title: Opening principles
summary: Move pawns to open lines for your rook and bishop, and get your king to safety early.
body: The opening is a race for space and safety. Every move should have a purpose.
Pawns in front of your rook and bishop open lines for them. Use those lines.
Your king starts in the middle of the back rank. Plan to move it into a castle soon.
This short line is a normal start. Each pawn push shows one idea.

notes.0: Sente opens the seventh file. This frees the bishop's diagonal.
notes.1: Gote mirrors the idea on the other side.
notes.2: The pawn on the second file opens a line for the rook.
notes.3: Both sides now have open lines. Next, decide where your king will live.

key: Open lines for your own pieces before you attack, and plan your king's safety early.

title: The bishop's diagonal
summary: Once the seventh-file pawn moves, the bishop on 8h can use the long diagonal.
body: The bishop moves on diagonals only. Look at its diagonals before you move it.
Your bishop starts on 8h. Its diagonal runs through 7g, 6f and on toward the centre.
Moving the pawn off 7g clears the first square of that diagonal.
Check where the bishop lands. It should attack something useful, not just sit.

notes.2: The bishop steps to 7g. Its diagonal now runs toward Gote's side of the board.

key: Clear the square in front of the bishop, then place it on the diagonal it needs.

title: Bishops face off
summary: When two bishops share a diagonal, the side to move can capture first, so count the recaptures.
body: After the bishop reaches 7g, Gote's bishop on 2b looks down the same diagonal.
The diagonal is open, so either bishop can take the other.
Whoever captures first wins the bishop unless the other side can recapture.
Here Gote takes first, but Sente's knight on 8i can jump to 7g and recapture, so the trade is even.

notes.3: Gote takes the bishop on 7g with its own bishop. Sente is down a bishop until it recaptures.
notes.4: The knight from 8i jumps to 7g and takes back. Bishops are traded evenly.

key: Before you put a piece on a shared line, count the attackers and defenders of that square.

title: Static rook and ranging rook
summary: A static rook stays on its home file, while a ranging rook slides sideways toward the centre.
body: The rook on 2h can stay where it is. This is a static rook plan.
Or it can slide sideways to attack. This is a ranging rook plan.
The two plans lead to very different castles and attacking chances.
This line shows the rook sliding along the 8th rank of the board from 2h to 5h.

notes.4: The rook moves from 2h to 5h along the rank. The path is clear, so the move is legal.

key: Choose your rook plan early, then build the castle and attack that match it.

title: The king walks to the corner
summary: An anaguma castle puts the king deep in a corner, and this demo shows only the king walking there.
body: A real anaguma is built around a king in the corner, with gold and silver pieces around it.
This lesson shows only the king's walk along the bottom rank to the 1i corner.
Corners are hard to attack. Few pieces can reach them, and the king has fewer escape squares to watch.

notes.0: The king leaves the centre of the back rank.

key: A king in a corner is hard to attack, but a real castle also needs its gold and silver pieces.

title: Castles and why they matter
summary: Yagura, Mino and the boat castle are built from gold and silver generals around the king.
body: A castle is a group of pieces around the king. The gold and silver generals do most of the work.
Yagura and Mino are two popular castles. Each one has its own shape and its own strengths.
The boat castle, funa-gakoi, is quick to build, but the king is less protected than in the stronger castles.
Every castle has a weak side. Learn where yours is, and where your opponent's is.

notes.1: Both sides have started a plan. Castles come next.

key: A castle works only if its gold and silver generals stay together and the king stays inside.

title: Building the Yagura castle
summary: The classic Static Rook fortress: king on 8h behind a wall of gold, gold and silver.
body: Yagura (矢倉, "fortress tower") is the traditional castle for Static Rook players, where your rook stays on its home file.
The finished shape has the king on 8h, golds on 7h and 6g, and a silver on 7g. The pawns on 7f and 6f sit in front like a roof.
It is very solid against attacks from the front, but it takes many moves to build, and it is weaker against attacks on the edge and from the side.
Gote's moves here are quiet developing moves so you can focus on Sente's castle.

notes.0: Open the bishop diagonal and make room for the silver to come up to 7g later.
notes.2: Pushing the 6th-file pawn gives the gold a square on 6g.
notes.4: The left gold steps up to 7h, next to where the king will live.
notes.6: The right gold starts its trip toward the king.
notes.8: Gold to 6g. Two golds now guard the castle's front.
notes.10: The silver heads for 7g by way of 6h.
notes.12: Silver on 7g: the wall is complete.
notes.14: The bishop gets out of the king's way, first to 7i, then to 6h.
notes.18: Now the king walks over: 6i, 7i, then 8h.
notes.22: King on 8h. The Yagura castle is finished: king 8h, golds 7h and 6g, silver 7g.

key: Yagura = king 8h, golds 7h and 6g, silver 7g. Strong in front, slow to build.

title: Building the Mino castle
summary: The Ranging Rook player's favourite castle: quick to build and hard to break from the side.
body: When you move your rook to the left side of the board (Ranging Rook), the right side is free for your king. The Mino castle (美濃囲い) uses that space.
The finished shape is king on 2h, silver on 3h, and golds on 4i and 5h. It takes only a few moves, which is why Ranging Rook players love it.
It holds up well against attacks from the side, but the head of the king (the squares above it) is a weak spot to watch.
Gote's moves here are quiet developing moves so you can focus on Sente's castle.

notes.2: The 6th-file pawn makes room for the rook's new home.
notes.4: Ranging Rook: the rook slides from 2h to 6h. For Sente this is the Fourth File Rook (shikenbisha), the most popular Ranging Rook opening.
notes.6: With the rook gone, the king walks right: 4h…
notes.12: The silver steps up to 3h, right next to the king.
notes.14: Gold from 6i to 5h. The Mino castle is complete: king 2h, silver 3h, golds 4i and 5h.

key: Mino = king 2h, silver 3h, golds 4i and 5h. Fast, and strong against side attacks.

title: The pawn drop threat
summary: A pawn dropped in front of a piece attacks it, so the piece must move or be defended.
body: A pawn attacks the square one step in front of it.
Dropping a pawn in front of an enemy piece threatens to capture that piece.
The target must move, be defended, or deal with the pawn.
Here the gold on 5b is only defended by the king. The pawn drop puts it under attack at once.

notes.0: The pawn on 5c attacks the gold on 5b. Gote must move the gold, defend it, or deal with the pawn.

key: A pawn drop in front of a piece creates an immediate threat.

title: Forks with the knight
summary: A knight attacks only two squares ahead, so one knight can attack two pieces at once.
body: A knight jumps two squares forward and one to the side. It has no other movement in front.
A knight on 4c attacks 5a and 3a. A king on 5a and a gold on 3a are both in trouble.
The king must move, so the gold on 3a falls.
Before you fork, check which two squares the knight can reach.

notes.0: The knight is dropped on 4c. It checks the king on 5a and attacks the gold on 3a.
notes.1: The king steps to 4b. It cannot stop the knight.
notes.2: The knight takes the gold on 3a and promotes, since a knight on the last rank has no moves.

key: A knight fork works best when the king is forced to move and cannot protect the other piece.

title: Edge pawn attacks
summary: Pushing an edge pawn is slow but can break a castle, so count the tempi before you commit.
body: Pawns on the edge files are often ignored. But they can be pushed to attack a castle.
Each push takes a move. Count whether your attack is faster than your opponent's.
This line shows two edge pawns pushed on the ninth file.

notes.0: The edge pawn on 9g moves to 9f.
notes.1: Gote answers with the matching edge pawn push.

key: An edge pawn attack is only useful when you can count its tempi against your opponent's defence.

title: Hisshi: the mate that can't be stopped
summary: A quiet move that isn't check, after which mate next move cannot be prevented.
body: In the endgame you often can't give checkmate right away. The next best thing is hisshi (必至): a move that threatens mate in such a way that no defence works.
Hisshi doesn't have to be check. That's what makes it powerful: it lets you finish the attack calmly.
It also decides races. If your opponent's king is in hisshi and yours is safe from immediate mate, you win even if they have more pieces.
Here Sente has a gold on 4b and a rook in hand. Sliding the gold to 3b is not check, but it takes away 2a and 2b from the king. Now a rook drop on the 1st file mates, and Gote has no way to stop it.

notes.0: G-3b. Not check, but the gold now covers 2a, 2b and 2c. The king is trapped on the 1st file, and Sente threatens a rook drop on it.
notes.1: Gote tries to run with K-1b. Every other move, like moving the lance, also loses to a rook drop.
notes.2: R*1d: the rook checks down the file, the gold covers every escape square, and nothing can block. Checkmate.

key: When you can't mate now, look for a quiet move that makes mate unstoppable.

title: Checkmate with a drop
summary: Many shogi games end with a piece dropped from hand right next to the enemy king.
body: Checkmate (tsumi) is a check the king cannot escape: it can't step away, nothing can capture the checking piece, and nothing can block it.
Pieces in hand make this easy to set up, because you can drop a gold or silver right beside the king where it is protected by another of your pieces.
Here Gote's king on 6a is hemmed in by its own gold and silver. A gold dropped on 5a, protected by Sente's promoted silver on 4b, ends the game.
The Puzzles tab has many more of these. They are the best way to learn to see mates.

notes.0: Gold drop on 5a: check. The king's own pieces block 7a, 7b and 6b, the gold covers 5b, and the promoted silver on 4b protects the gold, so the king can't take it. Checkmate.

key: Look for checks where the king has no free square and the checking piece is protected.
